analysis.one_liner: Allows Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 35 senators, died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare is currently barred from negotiating drug prices for its prescription drug benefit and must accept prices set by drug companies. This bill would erase that ban, letting the government negotiate prices directly and set reimbursement rates for drugs covered under the benefit. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of Medicare beneficiaries, roughly 43 million seniors and disabled Americans enrolled in the Medicare prescription drug benefit, would pay less out of pocket as negotiated prices replaced list prices. Taxpayers would also save, since Medicare funds a large share of the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the existing legal ban on Medicare interfering with private-plan drug negotiations, which is what currently prevents the government from negotiating prices directly [S3].
It authorizes the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to negotiate drug prices under the Medicare prescription drug benefit and to set a reimbursement price structure for covered drugs [S2].
Drug prices are a leading driver of Medicare costs; a government purchaser negotiating directly would use the buying power of a program covering tens of millions of seniors to push prices down [S2].
The change would take effect immediately upon enactment, with no phase-in period [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would see lower prices and thinner revenue on drugs sold through Medicare. Part D insurers and pharmacy middlemen could also see their margins squeezed if the government negotiates better prices than their private negotiations deliver.

drawbacks.text: Industry and economists' standard objection: lower prices negotiated by a single large purchaser could reduce the revenue drug companies earn, which they argue would mean less investment in future medicines [S3].

Some health-policy analysts argue Medicare can already influence prices through private Part D plans and that allowing government negotiation could let a single national price-setting process substitute for competition among private plans, a structural change with uncertain side effects [S3].
The bill sets no floor on negotiated prices and gives the Secretary broad discretion, meaning savings would depend heavily on how future administrations exercised the power [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real but one-sided: the public benefit of cheaper drugs for tens of millions of seniors and for the Treasury is large and direct, while the main cost is borne by one concentrated industry through lower revenue. The honest cost to weigh is the uncertain effect on future drug development, though other wealthy countries negotiate drug prices and still maintain pharmaceutical industries. The bill is a single, narrow change rather than a comprehensive drug-pricing overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat for two years without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 9, 2019, the opening days of the 116th Congress [S1].
Thirty-four senators from the Democratic caucus signed on as cosponsors, along with independent Senator Angus King; no Republican cosponsor joined [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor consideration during the entire two-year Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: the statutory ban on Medicare negotiation stayed in place, so drug prices for the Medicare program were untouched for another two years. The bill's model was eventually adopted in different form by a later Congress, but for this bill the outcome left the status quo fully intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers; prices stayed untouched

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 34 cosponsors from her caucus.

for.name: 34 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including party leaders such as the Senate Democratic Whip and the senior Senator from Massachusetts.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee, leaving it without a path to a vote.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained lobbying campaign throughout 2019-2020 against proposals to let Medicare negotiate drug prices, the policy this bill embodies.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 sponsors and cosponsors came from the Democratic caucus, including the one independent who caucuses with them; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past the Republican-chaired Finance Committee.

industries.note: The bill would let the government use Medicare's enormous buying power to negotiate prices down, directly cutting manufacturer revenue on a program covering tens of millions of people. Their interest in keeping the negotiation ban ran against beneficiaries and taxpayers paying higher prices.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill removes the statutory guarantee that the government will not interfere with their private negotiations, opening the door to direct government negotiation that could bypass or outperform them. Their cut of the drug pricing chain could shrink, though some savings might flow through their plans.

Greater price pressure on brand-name drugs typically speeds shifts toward cheaper generics, which would benefit from a negotiated price structure. Cheaper drugs for seniors are the same outcome they benefit from.
